plan.contextChunk: This figure stacks two panels, labeled (a) and (b), each plotting projectile trajectories that leave and return to the same level ground line. In panel (a) three parabolic arcs share one launch point and an angle marked 45 degrees, distinguished by velocity arrows at the origin labeled 30 m/s in orange, 40 m/s in purple, and 50 m/s in teal; a key at the upper right shows y up and x right. Dashed verticals drop from each apex, and three dimension bars beneath the ground line read R = 91.8 m, R = 163 m, and R = 255 m in that same order. Panel (b) instead fixes the speed, labeled v0 = 50 m/s, and varies the angle, with nested arcs at the origin marking 15, 45, and 75 degrees; only two dimension bars appear, R = 128 m ending at a dashed vertical where both the 15-degree and 75-degree curves land, and R = 255 m spanning the 45-degree curve. Matching each color-coded launch arrow to its own range bar isolates one launch parameter at a time. The layout supports the range relationship, in which range grows with the square of initial speed, peaks at 45 degrees, and repeats for complementary angles whose apex heights differ.

demo_steps.title: Same angle, changing speed
demo_steps.narration: In panel (a), the launch angle stays fixed at 45°. Drag the speed slider and watch the trajectory, apex guide, landing point, and range bar all stretch together.

demo_steps.title: Range grows as speed squared
demo_steps.narration: Increasing the speed from 30 m/s to 40 m/s to 50 m/s produces the textbook ranges 91.8 m, 163 m, and 255 m. The unequal spacing shows that range is proportional to v₀², not v₀.

demo_steps.title: Same speed, changing angle
demo_steps.narration: In panel (b), the speed is fixed at 50 m/s. Drag the angle slider and watch the projectile trade height for horizontal reach.

demo_steps.title: Complementary angles share range
demo_steps.narration: At 15° the projectile stays low; at the complementary angle 75° it rises much higher. Both land at the same range because the horizontal and vertical parts of the launch velocity are exchanged.

demo_steps.title: Maximum range at 45°
demo_steps.narration: At 45°, the balance between horizontal speed and time aloft gives the largest possible range for this launch speed.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: For level-ground projectile motion, speed controls the scale of the range quadratically, while angle controls the factor sin(2θ), making 45° the maximum and complementary angles equal in range.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the figure as two stacked 2D projectile panels on white background with thin black ground lines and dimension bars. Use orange for the low-speed or low-angle trajectory, purple for the middle 45° trajectory, and teal for the high-speed or high-angle trajectory. In panel (a), keep θ fixed at 45° and update a prominent current trajectory with its launch arrow, dashed apex guide, landing point, and range bar; faint reference curves at 30, 40, and 50 m/s may remain visible to match the textbook. In panel (b), keep v0 fixed at 50 m/s and update the current angle trajectory; also show a lighter complementary-angle trajectory and highlight the shared landing point when θ and 90°−θ have the same range. Range labels should round to the textbook values near 30, 40, and 50 m/s in panel (a), and near 15°, 45°, and 75° in panel (b).

authoredContext:
Note particularly that the equation is valid only for launch and impact on a horizontal surface. We see the range is directly proportional to the square of the initial speed v0 and sin2θ0, and it is inversely proportional to the acceleration of gravity. Thus, on the Moon, the range would be six times greater than on Earth for the same initial velocity. Furthermore, we see from the factor sin2θ0 that the range is maximum at 45°. These results are shown in the figure. In (a) we see that the greater the initial velocity, the greater the range. In (b), we see that the range is maximum at 45°. This is true only for conditions neglecting air resistance. If air resistance is considered, the maximum angle is somewhat smaller. It is interesting that the same range is found for two initial launch angles that sum to 90°. The projectile launched with the smaller angle has a lower apex than the higher angle, but they both have the same range.

Trajectories of projectiles on level ground. (a) The greater the initial speed v0, the greater the range for a given initial angle. (b) The effect of initial angle θ0 on the range of a projectile with a given initial speed. Note that the range is the same for initial angles of 15° and 75°, although the maximum heights of those paths are different.

Figure a shows the trajectories of projectiles launched at the same initial 45 degree angle above the horizontal and different initial velocities. The trajectories are shown from launch to landing back at the initial elevation. In orange is the trajectory for 30 meters per second, giving a range R (distance from launch to landing) of 91.8 m. In purple is the trajectory for 40 meters per second, giving a range R of 163 m. In blue is the trajectory for 50 meters per second, giving a range R of 255 m. The maximum height of the projectile increases with initial speed. Figure b shows the trajectories of projectiles launched at the same initial speed of 50 meters per second and different launch angles. The trajectories are shown from launch to landing back at the initial elevation. In orange is the trajectory for an angle of 15 degrees above the horizontal, giving a range R of 128 m. In purple is the trajectory for an angle of 45 degrees above the horizontal, giving a range R of 255 m. In blue is the trajectory for an angle of 75 degrees above the horizontal, giving a range R of 128 m, the same as for the 15 degree trajectory. The maximum height increases with launch angle.

When we speak of the range of a projectile on level ground, we assume R is very small compared with the circumference of Earth. If, however, the range is large, Earth curves away below the projectile and the acceleration resulting from gravity changes direction along the path. The range is larger than predicted by the range equation given earlier because the projectile has farther to fall than it would on level ground, as shown in the figure, which is based on a drawing in Newton’s Principia. If the initial speed is great enough, the projectile goes into orbit. Earth’s surface drops 5 m every 8000 m. In 1 s an object falls 5 m without air resistance. Thus, if an object is given a horizontal velocity of 8000 m/s (or 18,000 mi/hr) near Earth’s surface, it will go into orbit around the planet because the surface continuously falls away from the object. This is roughly the speed of the Space Shuttle in a low Earth orbit when it was operational, or any satellite in a low Earth orbit. These and other aspects of orbital motion, such as Earth’s rotation, are covered in greater depth in Gravitation.
